title: My, your, his: possession
description: Say whose something is, with pronouns and with nouns.

guide.title: Possessive pronouns
guide.text:
Each pronoun has a possessive form that goes before the noun and never changes, whatever the noun is:

naanu - ನನ್ನ (nanna) my; naavu - ನಮ್ಮ (namma) our; neenu - ನಿನ್ನ (ninna) your, familiar; neevu - ನಿಮ್ಮ (nimma) your, polite or plural; avanu - ಅವನ (avana) his; avalu - ಅವಳ (avala) her; avaru - ಅವರ (avara) their, or his/her respectfully; adu - ಅದರ (adara) its, of that; idu - ಇದರ (idara) of this; yaaru - ಯಾರ (yaara) whose.

Kannada speakers very often say namma ('our') where English says 'my' - for home, family, town and country: namma mane ('our house', even if you live alone), namma appa ('our father' = my father), namma ooru, namma bengalooru. Saying nanna mane is not wrong, but namma sounds warmer and more natural.

examples.english: their house / his or her house (respectful)

guide.title: Possessive of nouns: the ending -a
guide.text:
A noun is made possessive (the 'of' or apostrophe-s form, called the genitive) by adding -a. The possessor comes first, as with English 's: appana kaaru, 'father's car'. A linking sound is needed, and it depends on how the noun ends:

People whose name or title ends in -a add -na: appa - ಅಪ್ಪನ (appana) father's; snehita - ಸ್ನೇಹಿತನ (snehitana) friend's; raama - raamana.

Things ending in -a add -da: mara - ಮರದ (marada) of the tree; pustaka - pustakada.

Nouns ending in -i or -e add -ya: mane - ಮನೆಯ (maneya) of the house; hudugi - hudugiya, the girl's.

Nouns ending in -u drop the u and add -ina: ooru - ಊರಿನ (oorina) of the town; bengalooru - bengaloorina. Words for people ending in -u just replace u with a: avanu - avana, magalu (daughter) - magala.

In fast speech the ending is often dropped where the meaning is clear: mane baagilu, 'the house door'.

guide.title: Mine, yours, whose: adding -du
guide.text:
To use a possessive on its own, without a noun after it ('mine', 'yours', 'Ravi's'), add -du, which stands for 'thing': ನನ್ನದು (nannadu) mine, ನಮ್ಮದು (nammadu) ours, ನಿನ್ನದು (ninnadu) and ನಿಮ್ಮದು (nimmadu) yours, ಅವನದು (avanadu) his, ಅವಳದು (avaladu) hers, ಅವರದು (avaradu) theirs, ಯಾರದು (yaaradu) whose.

To ask a yes/no question add the long -aa: nimmadu + aa = ನಿಮ್ಮದಾ? (nimmadaa?) 'Is it yours?'. To deny, add alla: nannadu alla, 'it is not mine'.

phrases.note: The o in fon is long.
Could also be 'his house' or 'her house', said respectfully.
Also the natural way to say 'this is my home'.

phrases.english: The door of the house is open.
phrases.note: In speech often just mane baagilu.

phrases.english: What is the name of this?

phrases.note: A female friend is snehite (ಸ್ನೇಹಿತೆ); her possessive is snehiteya.

phrases.english: Your book is here. (to a friend)
phrases.note: ninna is the familiar 'your'; polite: nimma.
